title: The Museum Muddle
markdown:
The grand old museum hummed with a quiet sort of wonder, halls full of whispered ages. Asha, who kept things tidy and bright, polished the glass until it gleamed like sleepy eyes, and set the velvet ropes just so. The air smelled of polish and ancient dust, a shawl of a smell. Today the hum had a bewildered bleat in it, rippling through the floorboards.

Tumble, the museum’s unofficial mascot goat, peered into a display case. His beard twitched. The magnificent lion, usually prowling his savannah with regal confidence, stood confused beside a tank of shimmering jellyfish that pulsed with a soft inner light. The slithery snake, who preferred quiet shadowy corners and cool stone, was coiled unhappily near a proud eagle looking for a sky that was not there.

“Oh dear,” Asha said, voice soft as a moth. “A mischievous wind, scattering our friends.” She stroked Tumble’s fur.

Professor Imani’s voice floated down the hall, tweed smelling of old paper and meadow. Her eyes, sharp and kind, took in the pairings and crinkled.

“A rather creative turn overnight. A zoological jumble. Perhaps someone was experimenting with a very disorganized sort of organization.”

Tumble nudged a misplaced starfish. Velvety, wrong against the glass. “Baaaa. Like a song out of tune.”

“Often the best way to sort a muddle,” Imani said, “is to look very closely at what makes each creature unique. Gentle curiosity. Come. Follow the misplaced wonders.”

Their footsteps were soft on polish. Imani paused them at the lion. “Feel the strength in his form, even behind the glass. Powerful muscles. A steady stride. Now the jellyfish, tendrils like silk. Do you notice a difference in how they are built, deep inside?”

Asha tilted her head. “The lion feels solid. A strong frame, holding him up from the inside.” She remembered X-rays: bones like white ladders. “The jellyfish are almost wobbly water. Nothing hard inside at all.”

Imani’s eyes sparked. “Some animals — the lion, the eagle, even our slippery snake — have a backbone. A long line of small strong bones from head to tail-tip. Shape. Support. Movement. We call them vertebrates.”

Tumble nudged Asha’s hand, then pointed his nose at a delicate spider, legs poised. “Baaaa? No bones there?”

“Indeed not. Spider, starfish, jellyfish — no internal bony support. Invertebrates. Their strength might be a shell, or a soft form that can bend. Masters of their own designs.”

The museum felt less like a jumble and more like a puzzle waiting. Asha and Tumble looked at each other.

“So we put the ones with backbones together in their proper homes. And the ones without, in theirs.”

“That’s the idea. Not by forcing. By belonging. The right melody for each note.”

They did not hurry. Afternoon light moved a gold coin across the floor, and Asha watched it for the length of a breath, Tumble warm against her knee. Dust floated in the beam like a slow constellation. Then she guided the lion toward the savannah, mane catching the soft light, glass doors sighing. Tumble, surprisingly nimble for a goat with opinions about snacks, nudged the snake toward its shadowy rockery, where the stone was cool enough to please even a creature who had spent the morning next to an eagle. The eagle went back to its lofty perch, and one wing settled as if it had been holding its breath. Jellyfish and starfish returned to their water and drifted, silk and velvet in their right element. The spider found its web, threads shimmering, and seemed, if a spider can seem so, relieved not to be a neighbour to a lion.

As each settled, the museum’s hum returned, a gentle sigh through polish and old wood. Imani watched, satisfaction like a blanket. She did not pile on a sermon. The sorted cases said it: two grand families, backbone and no backbone, each perfect in its way. Tumble, who had a backbone of his own and knew it when he stretched, bleated as if to file himself with the lion, then thought better of climbing into the diorama.

Asha smoothed the velvet rope in front of the vertebrates and then the invertebrates, two quiet kingdoms under glass. Tumble rested his head on her knee. Late sun cast long warm shadows down the hall of skeletons and shells. Moonbeams would come later, silver on the floor, and all the creatures — sturdy-spined or soft-flowing — would be ready for their own quiet night. The polish smell settled again, familiar as a shawl.

Asha wondered, only wondered, what else in the building might belong together if you asked it about its insides. Tumble bleated, content, and the lion, in his right grass at last, looked as if he had remembered how to sleep.
characters: Asha (a museum helper), Tumble (a goat), Imani (a professor)
